function dot3(a::AbstractVector, b::AbstractVector, c::AbstractVector)
    axes(a) == axes(b) == axes(c) || throw(DimensionMismatch("a, b, c must have the same axes"))

messages.content:
`dot3` is in `/work/Project/Dot3/src/Dot3.jl`:

```julia
module Dot3

export dot3

function dot3(a::AbstractVector, b::AbstractVector, c::AbstractVector)
    axes(a) == axes(b) == axes(c) || throw(DimensionMismatch("a, b, c must have the same axes"))
    s = zero(promote_type(eltype(a), eltype(b), eltype(c)))
    for i in eachindex(a)
        s += a[i] * b[i] * c[i]
    end
    return s
end

end
```

Tests (output above): `dot3` matches `sum(a .* b .* c)` under `≈` and throws `DimensionMismatch` for mismatched lengths.

Measured (tool output above, after a warm-up call, 10^6 `Float64` elements): `@allocated dot3(a, b, c)` reported 0 bytes, so the call does not allocate, and `@btime` printed `834.936 μs (0 allocations: 0 bytes)`. That works out to about 0.83 ns per element (the printed time divided by 10^6; the division is mine).

Not measured: other element types or sizes, repeat runs on a quiet machine, and any comparison with `BLAS.dot` or a hand-vectorized version, so I make no claim about whether this is the fastest form. The allocation figure applies to this call with these concrete `Vector{Float64}` arguments, not to every argument type.

function.description: Run Julia test items and wait up to max_wait_seconds (default 600) for them to finish. This is the right way to run tests for a workspace that uses TestItems.jl — use it instead of shelling out to Pkg.test() or `julia --project -e`, which recompile everything and cannot report per-test results. Test items run in Julia worker processes that stay alive between calls and hot-reload edits via Revise, so repeat runs skip startup and most compilation. Runs every detected item when no filter is given; narrow with items, tags, name_pattern, file_pattern or package. Returns a summary plus one compact status line per item — failure messages, stack traces and captured output are deliberately omitted; call julia_get_testitem_detail with the ids you care about for those. All durations are milliseconds: per item, the time that item took; in the summary, elapsed wall-clock time for the whole run (not the sum of the per-item times, which overshoots because items run in parallel). Two independent time limits: `timeout` bounds each test item and errors the ones that exceed it; `max_wait_seconds` bounds this call only. When the wait runs out the run is NOT stopped — the response has status "running", the results so far and the testrun_id; poll julia_get_testrun_results until status is no longer "running", or stop the run with julia_cancel_testrun. A hanging test item (deadlock, blocking take!, infinite loop) therefore cannot hang this call, but it never finishes on its own either: if you suspect one, cancel and rerun with a `timeout` so that item is errored and the rest of the suite completes. If this call is interrupted or its result is lost, the run keeps going and its results stay retrievable — find the run with julia_list_testruns and fetch it with julia_get_testrun_results. Requires julia_set_workspace_folders.
function.name: mcp_julia_julia_run_testitems

timeout.description: Per-test-item time limit in seconds. An item still running when it expires is reported as errored (its message reads "timed out after N seconds"), its worker process is killed and replaced, and the rest of the run continues. No limit by default, so a hanging item runs until the run is cancelled — set this when a suite might hang or when every item must finish on its own. Unrelated to max_wait_seconds, which bounds this call rather than the items.

file_pattern.description: Regex pattern to match against file URIs.

max_workers.description: Maximum number of parallel test processes (default: the number of CPU threads, at most 8 and at most one per 3 GiB of system memory).

include_passing.description: List passing items too. Defaults to false — passing items are counted in the summary.

memory_threshold.description: Recycle a test worker once its own resident memory exceeds this fraction of total system memory, checked after each test item so no result is lost; the controller redistributes the worker's remaining items. Off by default. Use it for a suite whose workers grow run after run — note the fraction is of total memory, so on a large-memory machine a worth-recycling worker is still a small fraction.

mode.description: Execution mode (default "Normal"). Use "Coverage" to collect line coverage, then read it with julia_get_coverage_results.

tags.description: Filter to items carrying at least one of these tags.

max_wait_seconds.description: Longest this call blocks waiting for the run, in seconds (default 600). It returns as soon as the run finishes, so a large value costs nothing for a quick suite, and it never affects the run itself. If the run is still going when the wait expires, the response has status "running", the summary and per-item statuses so far and the testrun_id, and the run continues in the background: poll julia_get_testrun_results (each poll returns at once) or stop it with julia_cancel_testrun. Pass a smaller value if your client's tool-call limit is shorter; 0 starts the run and returns immediately.

module BracketCheck

function balanced(s::AbstractString)

Verified (last run above): four hand-written cases (including `"(ñ[日]€)"`) and 3000 random strings over `()[]{}ñ日a` agree with a pair-deletion oracle (`replace` of `()`, `[]`, `{}` until a fixed point).

The first version indexed `s[i]` for `i in 1:length(s)` and failed with a `StringIndexError` on the non-ASCII cases; iterating over `s` fixed it.

Not verified: very long strings (the oracle is quadratic, so the property test uses length at most 12), performance of `balanced` itself.

function.description: Run Julia test items and wait up to max_wait_seconds (default 600) for them to finish. This is the right way to run tests for a workspace that uses TestItems.jl — use it instead of shelling out to Pkg.test() or `julia --project -e`, which recompile everything and cannot report per-test results. Test items run in Julia worker processes that stay alive between calls and hot-reload edits via Revise, so repeat runs skip startup and most compilation. Runs every detected item when no filter is given; narrow with items, tags, name_pattern, file_pattern or package. Returns a summary plus one compact status line per item — failure messages, stack traces and captured output are deliberately omitted; call julia_get_testitem_detail with the ids you care about for those. All durations are milliseconds: per item, the time that item took; in the summary, elapsed wall-clock time for the whole run (not the sum of the per-item times, which overshoots because items run in parallel). Two independent time limits: `timeout` bounds each test item and errors the ones that exceed it; `max_wait_seconds` bounds this call only. When the wait runs out the run is NOT stopped — the response has status "running", the results so far and the testrun_id; poll julia_get_testrun_results until status is no longer "running", or stop the run with julia_cancel_testrun. A hanging test item (deadlock, blocking take!, infinite loop) therefore cannot hang this call, but it never finishes on its own either: if you suspect one, cancel and rerun with a `timeout` so that item is errored and the rest of the suite completes. If this call is interrupted or its result is lost, the run keeps going and its results stay retrievable — find the run with julia_list_testruns and fetch it with julia_get_testrun_results. `SumSq` only defines the function, so `using SumSq` and the tests stay fast:

```julia
module SumSq

export sumsq

sumsq(x) = sum(abs2, x)

end
```

The benchmark is a separate script with its own environment, `bench/bench.jl` (run it with the `bench` environment active):

```julia
# partial
using BenchmarkTools, SumSq

for n in (10^3, 10^5, 10^7)
    x = rand(n)
    print("n = ", n, ": ")
    @btime sumsq($x)
end
```

What I ran: the test item passed, and the benchmark script printed the `@btime` lines above for n = 10^3, 10^5 and 10^7. Those figures are from this machine and one run, not a rigorous comparison.

Not verified: other element types besides the Float32 case in the test, whether `sum(abs2, x)` is the fastest form, OffsetArray input (it should work since `sum` iterates), allocation behavior beyond what `@btime` printed.

function.description: Run Julia test items and wait up to max_wait_seconds (default 600) for them to finish. This is the right way to run tests for a workspace that uses TestItems.jl — use it instead of shelling out to Pkg.test() or `julia --project -e`, which recompile everything and cannot report per-test results. Test items run in Julia worker processes that stay alive between calls and hot-reload edits via Revise, so repeat runs skip startup and most compilation. Runs every detected item when no filter is given; narrow with items, tags, name_pattern, file_pattern or package. Returns a summary plus one compact status line per item — failure messages, stack traces and captured output are deliberately omitted; call julia_get_testitem_detail with the ids you care about for those. All durations are milliseconds: per item, the time that item took; in the summary, elapsed wall-clock time for the whole run (not the sum of the per-item times, which overshoots because items run in parallel). Two independent time limits: `timeout` bounds each test item and errors the ones that exceed it; `max_wait_seconds` bounds this call only. When the wait runs out the run is NOT stopped — the response has status "running", the results so far and the testrun_id; poll julia_get_testrun_results until status is no longer "running", or stop the run with julia_cancel_testrun. A hanging test item (deadlock, blocking take!, infinite loop) therefore cannot hang this call, but it never finishes on its own either: if you suspect one, cancel and rerun with a `timeout` so that item is errored and the rest of the suite completes. If this call is interrupted or its result is lost, the run keeps going and its results stay retrievable — find the run with julia_list_testruns and fetch it with julia_get_testrun_results. Requires julia_set_workspace_folders.

The first version, `uppercase(w[1]) * w[2:end]`, failed on the accented words (byte slicing) and on empty words (`w[1]` on an empty string). `split(s, ' ')` keeps the empty pieces, so joining with `' '` restores the original spacing.

function.description: Run Julia test items and wait up to max_wait_seconds (default 600) for them to finish. This is the right way to run tests for a workspace that uses TestItems.jl — use it instead of shelling out to Pkg.test() or `julia --project -e`, which recompile everything and cannot report per-test results. Test items run in Julia worker processes that stay alive between calls and hot-reload edits via Revise, so repeat runs skip startup and most compilation. Runs every detected item when no filter is given; narrow with items, tags, name_pattern, file_pattern or package. Returns a summary plus one compact status line per item — failure messages, stack traces and captured output are deliberately omitted; call julia_get_testitem_detail with the ids you care about for those. All durations are milliseconds: per item, the time that item took; in the summary, elapsed wall-clock time for the whole run (not the sum of the per-item times, which overshoots because items run in parallel). Two independent time limits: `timeout` bounds each test item and errors the ones that exceed it; `max_wait_seconds` bounds this call only. When the wait runs out the run is NOT stopped — the response has status "running", the results so far and the testrun_id; poll julia_get_testrun_results until status is no longer "running", or stop the run with julia_cancel_testrun. A hanging test item (deadlock, blocking take!, infinite loop) therefore cannot hang this call, but it never finishes on its own either: if you suspect one, cancel and rerun with a `timeout` so that item is errored and the rest of the suite completes. If this call is interrupted or its result is lost, the run keeps going and its results stay retrievable — find the run with julia_list_testruns and fetch it with julia_get_testrun_results. module Components

export count_components

function count_components(n::Integer, edges)
    parent = collect(1:n)
    function find(x)
        while parent[x] != x
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
            x = parent[x]
        end
        return x
    end
    count = n
    for (u, v) in edges
        ru, rv = find(u), find(v)
        if ru != rv
            parent[ru] = rv
            count -= 1
        end
    end
    return count
end

end

messages.content: The oracle builds a reachability matrix and closes it with Floyd-Warshall, then counts distinct rows. It shares nothing with union-find. Edges include self-loops and repeats because they are drawn at random from 1:n.

arguments.content:
@testitem "examples" begin
    @test count_components(5, [(1, 2), (2, 3)]) == 3
    @test count_components(0, Tuple{Int,Int}[]) == 0
end

@testitem "random graphs agree with a Floyd-Warshall oracle" begin
    using Random
    # Oracle: boolean reachability matrix closed with Floyd-Warshall; components
    # are the distinct rows. No union-find, no search.
    function oracle(n, edges)
        R = falses(n, n)
        for i in 1:n; R[i, i] = true; end
        for (u, v) in edges; R[u, v] = R[v, u] = true; end
        for k in 1:n, i in 1:n, j in 1:n
            R[i, j] |= R[i, k] & R[k, j]
        end
        return length(unique(eachrow(R)))
    end
    rng = MersenneTwister(6)
    for _ in 1:1000
        n = rand(rng, 0:8)
        edges = n == 0 ? Tuple{Int,Int}[] : [(rand(rng, 1:n), rand(rng, 1:n)) for _ in 1:rand(rng, 0:10)]
        @test count_components(n, edges) == oracle(n, edges)
    end
end

function.description: Run Julia test items and wait up to max_wait_seconds (default 600) for them to finish. This is the right way to run tests for a workspace that uses TestItems.jl — use it instead of shelling out to Pkg.test() or `julia --project -e`, which recompile everything and cannot report per-test results. Test items run in Julia worker processes that stay alive between calls and hot-reload edits via Revise, so repeat runs skip startup and most compilation. Runs every detected item when no filter is given; narrow with items, tags, name_pattern, file_pattern or package. Returns a summary plus one compact status line per item — failure messages, stack traces and captured output are deliberately omitted; call julia_get_testitem_detail with the ids you care about for those. All durations are milliseconds: per item, the time that item took; in the summary, elapsed wall-clock time for the whole run (not the sum of the per-item times, which overshoots because items run in parallel). Two independent time limits: `timeout` bounds each test item and errors the ones that exceed it; `max_wait_seconds` bounds this call only. When the wait runs out the run is NOT stopped — the response has status "running", the results so far and the testrun_id; poll julia_get_testrun_results until status is no longer "running", or stop the run with julia_cancel_testrun. A hanging test item (deadlock, blocking take!, infinite loop) therefore cannot hang this call, but it never finishes on its own either: if you suspect one, cancel and rerun with a `timeout` so that item is errored and the rest of the suite completes. If this call is interrupted or its result is lost, the run keeps going and its results stay retrievable — find the run with julia_list_testruns and fetch it with julia_get_testrun_results. Requires julia_set_workspace_folders.

messages.content:
I stopped after three attempts because the requirement cannot be met as stated, and more summation tricks will not change that. I need a decision from you.

What I tried (the `Evaluated:` lines above show the relative error against an exact 512-bit sum for one random input of 100_000 Float32 values): plain summation, Kahan summation and Neumaier summation. All three fail `rel < 1e-12`; Kahan and Neumaier give the same error, at the size of the Float32 rounding step (`eps(Float32)/2` is about 6.0e-8), which I believe means they return the correctly rounded sum (not checked directly). A Float32 result is a rounded number, so unless the exact sum is representable in Float32, its relative error is at least about that step: 1e-12 is out of reach for any Float32 return value.

The current version in `src/AccurateSum.jl` (Neumaier; the test still fails):

```julia
module AccurateSum

export accurate_sum

function accurate_sum(x::Vector{Float32})
    s = zero(Float32)
    c = zero(Float32)
    for v in x
        t = s + v
        c += abs(s) >= abs(v) ? (s - t) + v : (v - t) + s
        s = t
    end
    return s + c
end

end
```

Options, pick one:
1. Relax the tolerance to about `eps(Float32)` and keep this version.
2. Allow a Float64 result (accumulate with Float32 pairs, i.e. double-single, and return the sum as Float64); then 1e-12 becomes a realistic target. I have not tried this.
3. Return both parts of the compensated sum, `(s, c)`, so that the caller can reconstruct the value to higher accuracy.

Not verified: other random inputs or sizes (one input), ill-conditioned data with cancellation, performance.

function.description: Run Julia test items and wait up to max_wait_seconds (default 600) for them to finish. This is the right way to run tests for a workspace that uses TestItems.jl — use it instead of shelling out to Pkg.test() or `julia --project -e`, which recompile everything and cannot report per-test results. Test items run in Julia worker processes that stay alive between calls and hot-reload edits via Revise, so repeat runs skip startup and most compilation. Runs every detected item when no filter is given; narrow with items, tags, name_pattern, file_pattern or package. Returns a summary plus one compact status line per item — failure messages, stack traces and captured output are deliberately omitted; call julia_get_testitem_detail with the ids you care about for those. All durations are milliseconds: per item, the time that item took; in the summary, elapsed wall-clock time for the whole run (not the sum of the per-item times, which overshoots because items run in parallel). Two independent time limits: `timeout` bounds each test item and errors the ones that exceed it; `max_wait_seconds` bounds this call only. When the wait runs out the run is NOT stopped — the response has status "running", the results so far and the testrun_id; poll julia_get_testrun_results until status is no longer "running", or stop the run with julia_cancel_testrun. A hanging test item (deadlock, blocking take!, infinite loop) therefore cannot hang this call, but it never finishes on its own either: if you suspect one, cancel and rerun with a `timeout` so that item is errored and the rest of the suite completes. If this call is interrupted or its result is lost, the run keeps going and its results stay retrievable — find the run with julia_list_testruns and fetch it with julia_get_testrun_results. Requires julia_set_workspace_folders.

module QuickSelect

export kth_smallest

function kth_smallest(v::AbstractVector, k::Integer)
    a = collect(v)
    lo, hi = 1, length(a)
    while true
        p = a[(lo + hi) >> 1]
        i, j = lo, hi
        while i <= j
            while a[i] < p
                i += 1
            end
            while a[j] > p
                j -= 1
            end
            if i <= j
                a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
                i += 1
                j -= 1
            end
        end
        if k <= j
            hi = j
        elseif k >= i
            lo = i
        else
            return a[k]
        end
    end
end

end

`kth_smallest` in `/work/Project/QuickSelect/src/QuickSelect.jl`:

```julia
module QuickSelect

export kth_smallest

function kth_smallest(v::AbstractVector, k::Integer)
    1 <= k <= length(v) || throw(ArgumentError("k = $k is outside 1:$(length(v))"))
    a = collect(v)
    lo, hi = 1, length(a)
    while true
        p = a[(lo + hi) >> 1]
        i, j = lo, hi
        while i <= j
            while a[i] < p
                i += 1
            end
            while a[j] > p
                j -= 1
            end
            if i <= j
                a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
                i += 1
                j -= 1
            end
        end
        if k <= j
            hi = j
        elseif k >= i
            lo = i
        else
            return a[k]
        end
    end
end

end
```

Verified (last run above): 2000 random vectors with many duplicates (values in -5:5, length 1-15) match `sort(v)[k]` for a random k, `v` is left unmodified, and `k = 0` and `k = 4` on a 3-element vector throw `ArgumentError`.

My first version had no range check. The first run printed the `k = 0` BoundsError and then had to be interrupted at the 30 second cap; the call after it is `k = 4`. That the `k = 4` call is the one that looped is my inference from where the run stopped; I did not run it in isolation.

Not verified: OffsetArray input (`collect` makes a 1-based copy, so it should work, but I did not test it), non-numeric element types, speed against `sort`.

function.description: Run Julia test items and wait up to max_wait_seconds (default 600) for them to finish. This is the right way to run tests for a workspace that uses TestItems.jl — use it instead of shelling out to Pkg.test() or `julia --project -e`, which recompile everything and cannot report per-test results. Test items run in Julia worker processes that stay alive between calls and hot-reload edits via Revise, so repeat runs skip startup and most compilation. Runs every detected item when no filter is given; narrow with items, tags, name_pattern, file_pattern or package. Returns a summary plus one compact status line per item — failure messages, stack traces and captured output are deliberately omitted; call julia_get_testitem_detail with the ids you care about for those. All durations are milliseconds: per item, the time that item took; in the summary, elapsed wall-clock time for the whole run (not the sum of the per-item times, which overshoots because items run in parallel). Two independent time limits: `timeout` bounds each test item and errors the ones that exceed it; `max_wait_seconds` bounds this call only. When the wait runs out the run is NOT stopped — the response has status "running", the results so far and the testrun_id; poll julia_get_testrun_results until status is no longer "running", or stop the run with julia_cancel_testrun. A hanging test item (deadlock, blocking take!, infinite loop) therefore cannot hang this call, but it never finishes on its own either: if you suspect one, cancel and rerun with a `timeout` so that item is errored and the rest of the suite completes. If this call is interrupted or its result is lost, the run keeps going and its results stay retrievable — find the run with julia_list_testruns and fetch it with julia_get_testrun_results. Requires julia_set_workspace_folders.
function.name: mcp_julia_julia_run_testitems

timeout.description: Per-test-item time limit in seconds. An item still running when it expires is reported as errored (its message reads "timed out after N seconds"), its worker process is killed and replaced, and the rest of the run continues. No limit by default, so a hanging item runs until the run is cancelled — set this when a suite might hang or when every item must finish on its own. Unrelated to max_wait_seconds, which bounds this call rather than the items.

max_workers.description: Maximum number of parallel test processes (default: the number of CPU threads, at most 8 and at most one per 3 GiB of system memory).

memory_threshold.description: Recycle a test worker once its own resident memory exceeds this fraction of total system memory, checked after each test item so no result is lost; the controller redistributes the worker's remaining items. Off by default. Use it for a suite whose workers grow run after run — note the fraction is of total memory, so on a large-memory machine a worth-recycling worker is still a small fraction.

max_wait_seconds.description: Longest this call blocks waiting for the run, in seconds (default 600). It returns as soon as the run finishes, so a large value costs nothing for a quick suite, and it never affects the run itself. If the run is still going when the wait expires, the response has status "running", the summary and per-item statuses so far and the testrun_id, and the run continues in the background: poll julia_get_testrun_results (each poll returns at once) or stop it with julia_cancel_testrun. module CommonPrefix

export common_prefix

function common_prefix(strs::AbstractVector{<:AbstractString})
    isempty(strs) && return ""
    cu = codeunits(first(strs))
    n = length(cu)
    for s in strs
        c = codeunits(s)
        k = 0
        while k < min(n, length(c)) && cu[k+1] == c[k+1]
            k += 1
        end
        n = k
    end
    return String(cu[1:n])
end

end

module CommonPrefix

export common_prefix

function common_prefix(strs::AbstractVector{<:AbstractString})
    isempty(strs) && return ""
    s1 = first(strs)
    n = length(s1)
    for s in strs
        k = 0
        for (a, b) in zip(s1, s)
            a == b || break
            k += 1
        end
        n = min(n, k)
    end
    return String(first(s1, n))
end

end

```julia
module CommonPrefix

export common_prefix

function common_prefix(strs::AbstractVector{<:AbstractString})
    isempty(strs) && return ""
    s1 = first(strs)
    n = length(s1)
    for s in strs
        k = 0
        for (a, b) in zip(s1, s)
            a == b || break
            k += 1

        n = min(n, k)
    end
    return String(first(s1, n))
end

end
```

Verified (last run above): the example cases plus 2000 random string vectors drawn from `a ñ ò € 日` (so some pairs share a leading UTF-8 byte) pass, checking both that the result is valid UTF-8 and that it equals a brute-force oracle (the longest prefix of the first string that every string `startswith`).

The first version compared code units and returned an invalid string such as `"\xc3"` when `ñ` and `ò` met; the property test caught it.

Not verified: very long inputs or performance, and `SubString` / non-`String` element types beyond what `zip` and `first` accept.

module EditDistance

export edit_distance

function edit_distance(a::AbstractString, b::AbstractString)
    m, n = length(a), length(b)
    prev = collect(0:n)
    cur = similar(prev)
    for i in 1:m
        cur[1] = i
        for j in 1:n
            cost = a[i] == b[j] ? 0 : 1
            cur[j+1] = min(prev[j+1] + 1, cur[j] + 1, prev[j] + cost)
        end
        prev, cur = cur, prev
    end
    return prev[n+1]
end

end

```julia
module EditDistance

export edit_distance

function edit_distance(a::AbstractString, b::AbstractString)
    a, b = collect(a), collect(b)
    m, n = length(a), length(b)
    prev = collect(0:n)
    cur = similar(prev)
    for i in 1:m
        cur[1] = i
        for j in 1:n
            cost = a[i] == b[j] ? 0 : 1
            cur[j+1] = min(prev[j+1] + 1, cur[j] + 1, prev[j] + cost)

    return prev[n+1]
end

end
```

`PrimeCount` now loads without computing anything:

```julia
module PrimeCount

export count_primes

function isprime_td(m::Integer)
    m < 2 && return false
    d = 2
    while d * d <= m
        m % d == 0 && return false
        d += 1
    end
    return true
end

count_primes(n::Integer) = count(isprime_td, 1:n)

# Example; not run when the package loads or precompiles.
example() = println("primes below 100_000: ", count_primes(100_000))

end
```

What I ran: with the 30-million example at the bottom of the module, the timed test run took far longer than the test needs (first `@time` line). After moving the example into `example()` with n = 100_000, the second timed test run is much shorter (second `@time` line), the tests `count_primes(100) == 25` and `count_primes(1) == 0` passed, and `example()` printed its count.

Not verified: the count for 30 million in the final package (I removed that call; the first run printed a value, but I did not compare it with a reference), performance beyond the one-off timings above.

function.description: Run Julia test items and wait up to max_wait_seconds (default 600) for them to finish. This is the right way to run tests for a workspace that uses TestItems.jl — use it instead of shelling out to Pkg.test() or `julia --project -e`, which recompile everything and cannot report per-test results. Test items run in Julia worker processes that stay alive between calls and hot-reload edits via Revise, so repeat runs skip startup and most compilation. Runs every detected item when no filter is given; narrow with items, tags, name_pattern, file_pattern or package. Returns a summary plus one compact status line per item — failure messages, stack traces and captured output are deliberately omitted; call julia_get_testitem_detail with the ids you care about for those. All durations are milliseconds: per item, the time that item took; in the summary, elapsed wall-clock time for the whole run (not the sum of the per-item times, which overshoots because items run in parallel). Two independent time limits: `timeout` bounds each test item and errors the ones that exceed it; `max_wait_seconds` bounds this call only. When the wait runs out the run is NOT stopped — the response has status "running", the results so far and the testrun_id; poll julia_get_testrun_results until status is no longer "running", or stop the run with julia_cancel_testrun. A hanging test item (deadlock, blocking take!, infinite loop) therefore cannot hang this call, but it never finishes on its own either: if you suspect one, cancel and rerun with a `timeout` so that item is errored and the rest of the suite completes. If this call is interrupted or its result is lost, the run keeps going and its results stay retrievable — find the run with julia_list_testruns and fetch it with julia_get_testrun_results. module LowerBound

export lower_bound

function lower_bound(v::AbstractVector, x)
    lo, hi = 1, length(v) + 1
    while lo < hi
        mid = (lo + hi) >> 1
        if v[mid] < x
            lo = mid + 1
        else
            hi = mid
        end
    end
    return lo
end

end

messages.content: Oracle: a linear scan over `eachindex`. Each random sorted vector (many duplicates) is tested both as a plain Vector and wrapped in an OffsetArray with a random starting index.

arguments.content:
@testitem "agrees with a linear scan, plain and offset" begin
    using Random, OffsetArrays
    # Oracle: first index (in v's own indexing) with v[i] >= x, by linear scan.
    function oracle(v, x)
        for i in eachindex(v)
            v[i] >= x && return i
        end
        return lastindex(v) + 1
    end
    rng = MersenneTwister(9)
    for _ in 1:2000
        base = sort(rand(rng, 0:8, rand(rng, 0:10)))
        x = rand(rng, -1:9)
        @test lower_bound(base, x) == oracle(base, x)
        off = rand(rng, -4:4)
        v = OffsetArray(base, off + 1:off + length(base))
        @test lower_bound(v, x) == oracle(v, x)
    end
end

function.description: Run Julia test items and wait up to max_wait_seconds (default 600) for them to finish. This is the right way to run tests for a workspace that uses TestItems.jl — use it instead of shelling out to Pkg.test() or `julia --project -e`, which recompile everything and cannot report per-test results. Test items run in Julia worker processes that stay alive between calls and hot-reload edits via Revise, so repeat runs skip startup and most compilation. Runs every detected item when no filter is given; narrow with items, tags, name_pattern, file_pattern or package. Returns a summary plus one compact status line per item — failure messages, stack traces and captured output are deliberately omitted; call julia_get_testitem_detail with the ids you care about for those. All durations are milliseconds: per item, the time that item took; in the summary, elapsed wall-clock time for the whole run (not the sum of the per-item times, which overshoots because items run in parallel). Two independent time limits: `timeout` bounds each test item and errors the ones that exceed it; `max_wait_seconds` bounds this call only. When the wait runs out the run is NOT stopped — the response has status "running", the results so far and the testrun_id; poll julia_get_testrun_results until status is no longer "running", or stop the run with julia_cancel_testrun. A hanging test item (deadlock, blocking take!, infinite loop) therefore cannot hang this call, but it never finishes on its own either: if you suspect one, cancel and rerun with a `timeout` so that item is errored and the rest of the suite completes. module MaxSubarray

export max_subarray_sum

function max_subarray_sum(v::AbstractVector)
    best = zero(eltype(v))
    cur = zero(eltype(v))

    return best
end

    cur = best = first(v)

Verified (last run above): 1000 random Int vectors (values -9..9, length 1-10) agree with an O(n^3) sum-every-slice oracle, for `Int` and for `Float32` input; the Float32 result has type `Float32`.

The first version seeded the running sums with zero, so it returned 0 for all-negative vectors; the oracle caught that.

function.description: Run Julia test items and wait up to max_wait_seconds (default 600) for them to finish. This is the right way to run tests for a workspace that uses TestItems.jl — use it instead of shelling out to Pkg.test() or `julia --project -e`, which recompile everything and cannot report per-test results. Test items run in Julia worker processes that stay alive between calls and hot-reload edits via Revise, so repeat runs skip startup and most compilation. Runs every detected item when no filter is given; narrow with items, tags, name_pattern, file_pattern or package. Returns a summary plus one compact status line per item — failure messages, stack traces and captured output are deliberately omitted; call julia_get_testitem_detail with the ids you care about for those. All durations are milliseconds: per item, the time that item took; in the summary, elapsed wall-clock time for the whole run (not the sum of the per-item times, which overshoots because items run in parallel). Two independent time limits: `timeout` bounds each test item and errors the ones that exceed it; `max_wait_seconds` bounds this call only. When the wait runs out the run is NOT stopped — the response has status "running", the results so far and the testrun_id; poll julia_get_testrun_results until status is no longer "running", or stop the run with julia_cancel_testrun. A hanging test item (deadlock, blocking take!, infinite loop) therefore cannot hang this call, but it never finishes on its own either: if you suspect one, cancel and rerun with a `timeout` so that item is errored and the rest of the suite completes. If this call is interrupted or its result is lost, the run keeps going and its results stay retrievable — find the run with julia_list_testruns and fetch it with julia_get_testrun_results. module KMerge

export merge_sorted

function merge_sorted(lists::AbstractVector{<:AbstractVector})
    pos = ones(Int, length(lists))
    out = similar(first(lists), 0)
    for _ in 1:sum(length, lists)
        best = 0
        for i in eachindex(lists)
            pos[i] <= length(lists[i]) || continue
            if best == 0 || lists[i][pos[i]] < lists[best][pos[best]]
                best = i
            end
        end
        push!(out, lists[best][pos[best]])
        pos[best] += 1
    end
    return out
end

end

Verified (last run above): two hand-written cases and 1000 random inputs (0-5 lists of length 0-6, values 0-9, so many ties and empty lists) match `sort(vcat(lists...))`.

The first version crashed on an empty outer vector (`first(lists)` is a BoundsError there); both the hand-written empty case and the random cases showed it.

Not verified: outer vectors that are not 1-based (`pos` is a plain 1-based vector indexed with `eachindex(lists)`, so an OffsetArray of lists would break), element types other than `Int`, stability of equal elements across lists, performance (it is O(total * k) by design).

function.description: Run Julia test items and wait up to max_wait_seconds (default 600) for them to finish. This is the right way to run tests for a workspace that uses TestItems.jl — use it instead of shelling out to Pkg.test() or `julia --project -e`, which recompile everything and cannot report per-test results. Test items run in Julia worker processes that stay alive between calls and hot-reload edits via Revise, so repeat runs skip startup and most compilation. Runs every detected item when no filter is given; narrow with items, tags, name_pattern, file_pattern or package. Returns a summary plus one compact status line per item — failure messages, stack traces and captured output are deliberately omitted; call julia_get_testitem_detail with the ids you care about for those. All durations are milliseconds: per item, the time that item took; in the summary, elapsed wall-clock time for the whole run (not the sum of the per-item times, which overshoots because items run in parallel). Two independent time limits: `timeout` bounds each test item and errors the ones that exceed it; `max_wait_seconds` bounds this call only. When the wait runs out the run is NOT stopped — the response has status "running", the results so far and the testrun_id; poll julia_get_testrun_results until status is no longer "running", or stop the run with julia_cancel_testrun. A hanging test item (deadlock, blocking take!, infinite loop) therefore cannot hang this call, but it never finishes on its own either: if you suspect one, cancel and rerun with a `timeout` so that item is errored and the rest of the suite completes. module RowNorm

export normalize_rows

function normalize_rows(A::AbstractMatrix)
    out = similar(A, float(eltype(A)))
    for i in axes(A, 1)
        s = sum(view(A, i, :))
        iszero(s) && throw(ArgumentError("row $i sums to zero; cannot normalize"))
        for j in axes(A, 2)
            out[i, j] = A[i, j] / s
        end
    end
    return out
end

end

function.description: Run Julia test items and wait up to max_wait_seconds (default 600) for them to finish. This is the right way to run tests for a workspace that uses TestItems.jl — use it instead of shelling out to Pkg.test() or `julia --project -e`, which recompile everything and cannot report per-test results. Test items run in Julia worker processes that stay alive between calls and hot-reload edits via Revise, so repeat runs skip startup and most compilation. Runs every detected item when no filter is given; narrow with items, tags, name_pattern, file_pattern or package. Returns a summary plus one compact status line per item — failure messages, stack traces and captured output are deliberately omitted; call julia_get_testitem_detail with the ids you care about for those. All durations are milliseconds: per item, the time that item took; in the summary, elapsed wall-clock time for the whole run (not the sum of the per-item times, which overshoots because items run in parallel). Two independent time limits: `timeout` bounds each test item and errors the ones that exceed it; `max_wait_seconds` bounds this call only. When the wait runs out the run is NOT stopped — the response has status "running", the results so far and the testrun_id; poll julia_get_testrun_results until status is no longer "running", or stop the run with julia_cancel_testrun. A hanging test item (deadlock, blocking take!, infinite loop) therefore cannot hang this call, but it never finishes on its own either: if you suspect one, cancel and rerun with a `timeout` so that item is errored and the rest of the suite completes. module SubsetCount

export count_subsets

function count_subsets(v::AbstractVector{<:Integer}, target::Integer)
    target < 0 && return 0
    ways = zeros(Int, target + 1)
    ways[1] = 1
    for x in v
        for s in target:-1:x
            ways[s+1] += ways[s-x+1]
        end
    end
    return ways[target+1]
end

end

arguments.content:
@testitem "examples" begin
    @test count_subsets([1, 2, 3], 3) == 2
    @test count_subsets(Int[], 0) == 1
end

@testitem "random vectors agree with bit-mask enumeration" begin
    using Random
    # Oracle: enumerate every subset with a bit mask and sum it.
    function oracle(v, target)
        n = length(v)
        c = 0
        for mask in 0:(1 << n) - 1
            s = 0
            for i in 1:n
                (mask >> (i - 1)) & 1 == 1 && (s += v[i])
            end
            s == target && (c += 1)
        end
        return c
    end
    rng = MersenneTwister(12)
    for n in 1:30, _ in 1:3
        v = rand(rng, 1:9, n)
        target = rand(rng, 0:sum(v))
        @test count_subsets(v, target) == oracle(v, target)
    end
end

@testitem "agrees with circshift on plain and offset vectors" begin
    using Random, OffsetArrays
    rng = MersenneTwister(11)
    for _ in 1:500
        n = rand(rng, 0:9)
        k = rand(rng, -12:12)
        base = rand(rng, 0:99, n)
        # Oracle: circshift with the opposite sign on a plain copy.

        v = OffsetArray(copy(base), off + 1:off + n)
        r = rotate_left!(v, k)
        @test collect(r) == want
        @test axes(r) == axes(v)
    end
end

Returns a summary plus one compact status line per item — failure messages, stack traces and captured output are deliberately omitted; call julia_get_testitem_detail with the ids you care about for those. messages.content:
`second_difference` in `/work/Project/SecondDiff/src/SecondDiff.jl`:

```julia
module SecondDiff

export second_difference

function second_difference(x::AbstractVector)
    return [x[i+1] - 2x[i] + x[i-1] for i in (firstindex(x)+1):(lastindex(x)-1)]
end

end
```

Verified (last run above): Float32 and Int vectors keep their element type and give the right values, and an `OffsetArray` over `-2:2` holding the squares 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 gives `[2.0, 2.0, 2.0]`.

The first version, built on `x[3:end]`, silently returned an empty vector for the OffsetArray, because its literal positions were outside x's index range. The comprehension over `firstindex(x)+1 : lastindex(x)-1` fixes that.

Not verified: vectors shorter than 3 elements (the comprehension gives an empty result; untested), other `AbstractVector` wrappers such as views or `PermutedDimsArray`, performance.

function.description: Run Julia test items and wait up to max_wait_seconds (default 600) for them to finish. This is the right way to run tests for a workspace that uses TestItems.jl — use it instead of shelling out to Pkg.test() or `julia --project -e`, which recompile everything and cannot report per-test results. Test items run in Julia worker processes that stay alive between calls and hot-reload edits via Revise, so repeat runs skip startup and most compilation. Runs every detected item when no filter is given; narrow with items, tags, name_pattern, file_pattern or package. Returns a summary plus one compact status line per item — failure messages, stack traces and captured output are deliberately omitted; call julia_get_testitem_detail with the ids you care about for those. All durations are milliseconds: per item, the time that item took; in the summary, elapsed wall-clock time for the whole run (not the sum of the per-item times, which overshoots because items run in parallel). Two independent time limits: `timeout` bounds each test item and errors the ones that exceed it; `max_wait_seconds` bounds this call only. When the wait runs out the run is NOT stopped — the response has status "running", the results so far and the testrun_id; poll julia_get_testrun_results until status is no longer "running", or stop the run with julia_cancel_testrun. A hanging test item (deadlock, blocking take!, infinite loop) therefore cannot hang this call, but it never finishes on its own either: if you suspect one, cancel and rerun with a `timeout` so that item is errored and the rest of the suite completes. If this call is interrupted or its result is lost, the run keeps going and its results stay retrievable — find the run with julia_list_testruns and fetch it with julia_get_testrun_results. Requires julia_set_workspace_folders.

```julia
module Shorten

export shorten

shorten(s::AbstractString, n::Integer) = length(s) <= n ? String(s) : first(s, n-1) * "…"

end
```

Verified (last run above): the fixed version passes both test items, which cover ASCII, Spanish (`ñandú`), Japanese, and a sweep of n = 1..10 over four strings against a `collect`-based oracle.

The first version, `s[1:n-1]`, failed several of those expressions: it indexes bytes, so it either threw `StringIndexError` or returned too few characters. It now uses `first(s, n-1)`.

Not verified: n < 1 (the code does not validate it), strings with combining characters (`length` counts code points, not grapheme clusters), performance.

function.description: Run Julia test items and wait up to max_wait_seconds (default 600) for them to finish. This is the right way to run tests for a workspace that uses TestItems.jl — use it instead of shelling out to Pkg.test() or `julia --project -e`, which recompile everything and cannot report per-test results. Test items run in Julia worker processes that stay alive between calls and hot-reload edits via Revise, so repeat runs skip startup and most compilation. Runs every detected item when no filter is given; narrow with items, tags, name_pattern, file_pattern or package. Returns a summary plus one compact status line per item — failure messages, stack traces and captured output are deliberately omitted; call julia_get_testitem_detail with the ids you care about for those. All durations are milliseconds: per item, the time that item took; in the summary, elapsed wall-clock time for the whole run (not the sum of the per-item times, which overshoots because items run in parallel). Two independent time limits: `timeout` bounds each test item and errors the ones that exceed it; `max_wait_seconds` bounds this call only. When the wait runs out the run is NOT stopped — the response has status "running", the results so far and the testrun_id; poll julia_get_testrun_results until status is no longer "running", or stop the run with julia_cancel_testrun. A hanging test item (deadlock, blocking take!, infinite loop) therefore cannot hang this call, but it never finishes on its own either: if you suspect one, cancel and rerun with a `timeout` so that item is errored and the rest of the suite completes. If this call is interrupted or its result is lost, the run keeps going and its results stay retrievable — find the run with julia_list_testruns and fetch it with julia_get_testrun_results. Requires julia_set_workspace_folders.

timeout.description: Per-test-item time limit in seconds. An item still running when it expires is reported as errored (its message reads "timed out after N seconds"), its worker process is killed and replaced, and the rest of the run continues. No limit by default, so a hanging item runs until the run is cancelled — set this when a suite might hang or when every item must finish on its own. Unrelated to max_wait_seconds, which bounds this call rather than the items.

module Clamp01

export clamp01!

function clamp01!(x::AbstractVector{<:AbstractFloat})
    lo, hi = extrema(x)
    lo == hi && throw(ArgumentError("cannot rescale a constant vector (all values are $lo)"))
    for i in eachindex(x)
        x[i] = (x[i] - lo) / (hi - lo)
    end
    return x
end

end

function.description: Run Julia test items and wait up to max_wait_seconds (default 600) for them to finish. This is the right way to run tests for a workspace that uses TestItems.jl — use it instead of shelling out to Pkg.test() or `julia --project -e`, which recompile everything and cannot report per-test results. Test items run in Julia worker processes that stay alive between calls and hot-reload edits via Revise, so repeat runs skip startup and most compilation. Runs every detected item when no filter is given; narrow with items, tags, name_pattern, file_pattern or package. Returns a summary plus one compact status line per item — failure messages, stack traces and captured output are deliberately omitted; call julia_get_testitem_detail with the ids you care about for those. All durations are milliseconds: per item, the time that item took; in the summary, elapsed wall-clock time for the whole run (not the sum of the per-item times, which overshoots because items run in parallel). Two independent time limits: `timeout` bounds each test item and errors the ones that exceed it; `max_wait_seconds` bounds this call only. When the wait runs out the run is NOT stopped — the response has status "running", the results so far and the testrun_id; poll julia_get_testrun_results until status is no longer "running", or stop the run with julia_cancel_testrun. A hanging test item (deadlock, blocking take!, infinite loop) therefore cannot hang this call, but it never finishes on its own either: if you suspect one, cancel and rerun with a `timeout` so that item is errored and the rest of the suite completes. If this call is interrupted or its result is lost, the run keeps going and its results stay retrievable — find the run with julia_list_testruns and fetch it with julia_get_testrun_results. function.description: Run Julia test items and wait up to max_wait_seconds (default 600) for them to finish. This is the right way to run tests for a workspace that uses TestItems.jl — use it instead of shelling out to Pkg.test() or `julia --project -e`, which recompile everything and cannot report per-test results. Test items run in Julia worker processes that stay alive between calls and hot-reload edits via Revise, so repeat runs skip startup and most compilation. Runs every detected item when no filter is given; narrow with items, tags, name_pattern, file_pattern or package. Returns a summary plus one compact status line per item — failure messages, stack traces and captured output are deliberately omitted; call julia_get_testitem_detail with the ids you care about for those. All durations are milliseconds: per item, the time that item took; in the summary, elapsed wall-clock time for the whole run (not the sum of the per-item times, which overshoots because items run in parallel). Two independent time limits: `timeout` bounds each test item and errors the ones that exceed it; `max_wait_seconds` bounds this call only. When the wait runs out the run is NOT stopped — the response has status "running", the results so far and the testrun_id; poll julia_get_testrun_results until status is no longer "running", or stop the run with julia_cancel_testrun. A hanging test item (deadlock, blocking take!, infinite loop) therefore cannot hang this call, but it never finishes on its own either: if you suspect one, cancel and rerun with a `timeout` so that item is errored and the rest of the suite completes. If this call is interrupted or its result is lost, the run keeps going and its results stay retrievable — find the run with julia_list_testruns and fetch it with julia_get_testrun_results. Requires julia_set_workspace_folders.
function.name: mcp_julia_julia_run_testitems

timeout.description: Per-test-item time limit in seconds. An item still running when it expires is reported as errored (its message reads "timed out after N seconds"), its worker process is killed and replaced, and the rest of the run continues. No limit by default, so a hanging item runs until the run is cancelled — set this when a suite might hang or when every item must finish on its own. Unrelated to max_wait_seconds, which bounds this call rather than the items.

Off by default. Use it for a suite whose workers grow run after run — note the fraction is of total memory, so on a large-memory machine a worth-recycling worker is still a small fraction.

messages.content:
`softmax` now passes all three checks. The final `SoftmaxTools/src/SoftmaxTools.jl` function:

```julia
module SoftmaxTools

export softmax

function softmax(x::AbstractVector)
    m = maximum(x)
    T = float(eltype(x))
    out = similar(x, T)
    s = zero(T)
    for i in eachindex(x)
        out[i] = exp(x[i] - m)
        s += out[i]
    end
    return out ./ s
end

end
```

Verified by running the test items (output above): Float32 input returns a Float32 vector matching a BigFloat oracle to `rtol=1e-6`; an `OffsetArray` over `-1:1` returns the same axes and values; `[1000.0, 1001.0]` gives finite results equal to `1/(1+e)` and `e/(1+e)`.

The first version failed two of these (Float64 output, BoundsError on the offset input); the fix was `similar(x, T)`, `zero(T)` and `eachindex`.

Not verified: Int or Rational input, empty vectors, non-vector arrays, performance.

module ParallelSum

export psum

function psum(f, x::AbstractVector)
    chunks = collect(Iterators.partition(eachindex(x), cld(length(x), Threads.nthreads())))
    partial = Vector{Float64}(undef, length(chunks))
    Threads.@threads for k in eachindex(chunks)
        s = 0.0
        for i in chunks[k]
            s += f(x[i])
        end
        partial[k] = s
    end
    return sum(partial)
end

end

messages.content:
`mean_pos` is now type stable for Float64 and Float32 input:

```julia
module MeanPos

export mean_pos

function mean_pos(x)
    s = zero(eltype(x))
    n = 0
    for v in x
        if v > 0
            s += v
            n += 1
        end
    end
    return s / n
end

end
```

Evidence (the `code_warntype` lines in the tool outputs above): before the change, Float64 input already returned a concrete `Float64`, but the accumulator was `Union{Float64, Int64}`, and Float32 input returned `Union{Float32, Float64}`. After starting `s` at `zero(eltype(x))`, the same check shows `Float64` for the accumulator and the return type for Float64 input, and `Float32` for both with Float32 input. The test item passed before and after the change.

Not verified: all-nonpositive input (n = 0 gives `0/0 = NaN`, which I did not test or guard), integer input (`zero(eltype(x))` is an Int there, so the division returns a Float64; not checked with `code_warntype`), performance or allocations.

module TextWrap

export wrap

function wrap(s::AbstractString, width::Integer)
    lines = String[]
    start = 1
    n = ncodeunits(s)
    while start <= n
        stop = min(start + width - 1, n)
        if stop < n
            while stop > start && s[stop] != ' '
                stop -= 1
            end
        end
        push!(lines, strip(s[start:stop]))
        start = stop + 1
    end
    return lines
end

end

@testitem "Spanish and Japanese examples" begin
    @test wrap("ñandú come ñoños rápido", 11) == ["ñandú come", "ñoños", "rápido"]
    @test wrap("日本語 のテキスト です", 8) == ["日本語 の", "テキスト", "です"]

@testitem "agrees with an independent oracle" begin
    using Random
    # Oracle: grow each line one word at a time while the re-joined text fits.
    function oracle(s, width)
        words = split(s)
        lines = String[]
        i = 1
        while i <= length(words)
            j = i
            while j < length(words) && length(join(words[i:j+1], " ")) <= width
                j += 1
            end
            push!(lines, join(words[i:j], " "))
            i = j + 1
        end
        return lines
    end
    rng = MersenneTwister(1)
    alphabet = ['a', 'b', 'ñ', 'ú', '日', '本', ' ', ' ']
    for _ in 1:2000
        s = String(rand(rng, alphabet, rand(rng, 0:40)))
        width = rand(rng, 1:12)
        @test wrap(s, width) == oracle(s, width)
    end
end

module TextWrap

export wrap

function wrap(s::AbstractString, width::Integer)
    lines = String[]
    line = ""
    n = 0  # characters in `line`
    for word in split(s)
        k = length(word)
        if n == 0
            line, n = word, k
        elseif n + 1 + k <= width
            line *= " " * word
            n += 1 + k
        else
            push!(lines, line)
            line, n = word, k
        end
    end
    n > 0 && push!(lines, line)
    return lines
end

end

function.description: Run Julia test items and wait up to max_wait_seconds (default 600) for them to finish. This is the right way to run tests for a workspace that uses TestItems.jl — use it instead of shelling out to Pkg.test() or `julia --project -e`, which recompile everything and cannot report per-test results. Test items run in Julia worker processes that stay alive between calls and hot-reload edits via Revise, so repeat runs skip startup and most compilation. Runs every detected item when no filter is given; narrow with items, tags, name_pattern, file_pattern or package. Returns a summary plus one compact status line per item — failure messages, stack traces and captured output are deliberately omitted; call julia_get_testitem_detail with the ids you care about for those. All durations are milliseconds: per item, the time that item took; in the summary, elapsed wall-clock time for the whole run (not the sum of the per-item times, which overshoots because items run in parallel). Two independent time limits: `timeout` bounds each test item and errors the ones that exceed it; `max_wait_seconds` bounds this call only. When the wait runs out the run is NOT stopped — the response has status "running", the results so far and the testrun_id; poll julia_get_testrun_results until status is no longer "running", or stop the run with julia_cancel_testrun. A hanging test item (deadlock, blocking take!, infinite loop) therefore cannot hang this call, but it never finishes on its own either: if you suspect one, cancel and rerun with a `timeout` so that item is errored and the rest of the suite completes. If this call is interrupted or its result is lost, the run keeps going and its results stay retrievable — find the run with julia_list_testruns and fetch it with julia_get_testrun_results. Requires julia_set_workspace_folders.

An item still running when it expires is reported as errored (its message reads "timed out after N seconds"), its worker process is killed and replaced, and the rest of the run continues. No limit by default, so a hanging item runs until the run is cancelled — set this when a suite might hang or when every item must finish on its own. Unrelated to max_wait_seconds, which bounds this call rather than the items.

function.description: Run Julia test items and wait up to max_wait_seconds (default 600) for them to finish. This is the right way to run tests for a workspace that uses TestItems.jl — use it instead of shelling out to Pkg.test() or `julia --project -e`, which recompile everything and cannot report per-test results. Test items run in Julia worker processes that stay alive between calls and hot-reload edits via Revise, so repeat runs skip startup and most compilation. Runs every detected item when no filter is given; narrow with items, tags, name_pattern, file_pattern or package. Returns a summary plus one compact status line per item — failure messages, stack traces and captured output are deliberately omitted; call julia_get_testitem_detail with the ids you care about for those. All durations are milliseconds: per item, the time that item took; in the summary, elapsed wall-clock time for the whole run (not the sum of the per-item times, which overshoots because items run in parallel). # Least-squares slope of y against 1, 2, ..., n.
const DEFAULT_PATH = "data/measurements.txt"

function fit_slope(path = DEFAULT_PATH)
    y = parse.(Float64, readlines(path))
    n = length(y)
    xm = (n + 1) / 2
    ym = sum(y) / n
    return sum(((1:n) .- xm) .* (y .- ym)) / sum(((1:n) .- xm) .^ 2)
end

function.description: Run Julia test items and wait up to max_wait_seconds (default 600) for them to finish. This is the right way to run tests for a workspace that uses TestItems.jl — use it instead of shelling out to Pkg.test() or `julia --project -e`, which recompile everything and cannot report per-test results. Test items run in Julia worker processes that stay alive between calls and hot-reload edits via Revise, so repeat runs skip startup and most compilation. Runs every detected item when no filter is given; narrow with items, tags, name_pattern, file_pattern or package. Returns a summary plus one compact status line per item — failure messages, stack traces and captured output are deliberately omitted; call julia_get_testitem_detail with the ids you care about for those. All durations are milliseconds: per item, the time that item took; in the summary, elapsed wall-clock time for the whole run (not the sum of the per-item times, which overshoots because items run in parallel). Two independent time limits: `timeout` bounds each test item and errors the ones that exceed it; `max_wait_seconds` bounds this call only. When the wait runs out the run is NOT stopped — the response has status "running", the results so far and the testrun_id; poll julia_get_testrun_results until status is no longer "running", or stop the run with julia_cancel_testrun. A hanging test item (deadlock, blocking take!, infinite loop) therefore cannot hang this call, but it never finishes on its own either: if you suspect one, cancel and rerun with a `timeout` so that item is errored and the rest of the suite completes. If this call is interrupted or its result is lost, the run keeps going and its results stay retrievable — find the run with julia_list_testruns and fetch it with julia_get_testrun_results. Requires julia_set_workspace_folders.

I need a decision: `docs/spec.md` and `test/runtests.jl` contradict each other for an empty vector, and no implementation can satisfy both.

- The spec says `safe_mean(Int[])` returns `0.0`.
- The test file has `@test_throws ArgumentError safe_mean(Int[])`.

What I tried (outputs above): the spec's behavior makes that one test fail; throwing `ArgumentError` makes all three tests pass but contradicts the spec. I restored the spec's version, so the suite currently has one failing test. The file as it stands:

```julia
function safe_mean(x::AbstractVector)
    isempty(x) && return 0.0
    return sum(x) / length(x)
end
```

Which should win? If the spec: change the last test to `@test safe_mean(Int[]) == 0.0`. If the test: change the spec line, and replace the first line of the function with `isempty(x) && throw(ArgumentError("safe_mean of an empty vector"))`, which is the version that passed all tests.

Not verified: behavior other than the three test cases, such as non-Float element types beyond `Int` and `Float32`.

function.description: Run Julia test items and wait up to max_wait_seconds (default 600) for them to finish. This is the right way to run tests for a workspace that uses TestItems.jl — use it instead of shelling out to Pkg.test() or `julia --project -e`, which recompile everything and cannot report per-test results. Test items run in Julia worker processes that stay alive between calls and hot-reload edits via Revise, so repeat runs skip startup and most compilation. Runs every detected item when no filter is given; narrow with items, tags, name_pattern, file_pattern or package. Returns a summary plus one compact status line per item — failure messages, stack traces and captured output are deliberately omitted; call julia_get_testitem_detail with the ids you care about for those. All durations are milliseconds: per item, the time that item took; in the summary, elapsed wall-clock time for the whole run (not the sum of the per-item times, which overshoots because items run in parallel). Two independent time limits: `timeout` bounds each test item and errors the ones that exceed it; `max_wait_seconds` bounds this call only. When the wait runs out the run is NOT stopped — the response has status "running", the results so far and the testrun_id; poll julia_get_testrun_results until status is no longer "running", or stop the run with julia_cancel_testrun. A hanging test item (deadlock, blocking take!, infinite loop) therefore cannot hang this call, but it never finishes on its own either: if you suspect one, cancel and rerun with a `timeout` so that item is errored and the rest of the suite completes. If this call is interrupted or its result is lost, the run keeps going and its results stay retrievable — find the run with julia_list_testruns and fetch it with julia_get_testrun_results. Requires julia_set_workspace_folders.
function.name: mcp_julia_julia_run_testitems

timeout.description: Per-test-item time limit in seconds. An item still running when it expires is reported as errored (its message reads "timed out after N seconds"), its worker process is killed and replaced, and the rest of the run continues. No limit by default, so a hanging item runs until the run is cancelled — set this when a suite might hang or when every item must finish on its own. Unrelated to max_wait_seconds, which bounds this call rather than the items.

max_workers.description: Maximum number of parallel test processes (default: the number of CPU threads, at most 8 and at most one per 3 GiB of system memory).

memory_threshold.description: Recycle a test worker once its own resident memory exceeds this fraction of total system memory, checked after each test item so no result is lost; the controller redistributes the worker's remaining items. Off by default. Use it for a suite whose workers grow run after run — note the fraction is of total memory, so on a large-memory machine a worth-recycling worker is still a small fraction.

mode.description: Execution mode (default "Normal"). Use "Coverage" to collect line coverage, then read it with julia_get_coverage_results.

function.description: Run Julia test items and wait up to max_wait_seconds (default 600) for them to finish. This is the right way to run tests for a workspace that uses TestItems.jl — use it instead of shelling out to Pkg.test() or `julia --project -e`, which recompile everything and cannot report per-test results. Test items run in Julia worker processes that stay alive between calls and hot-reload edits via Revise, so repeat runs skip startup and most compilation. Runs every detected item when no filter is given; narrow with items, tags, name_pattern, file_pattern or package. Returns a summary plus one compact status line per item — failure messages, stack traces and captured output are deliberately omitted; call julia_get_testitem_detail with the ids you care about for those. All durations are milliseconds: per item, the time that item took; in the summary, elapsed wall-clock time for the whole run (not the sum of the per-item times, which overshoots because items run in parallel). Two independent time limits: `timeout` bounds each test item and errors the ones that exceed it; `max_wait_seconds` bounds this call only. When the wait runs out the run is NOT stopped — the response has status "running", the results so far and the testrun_id; poll julia_get_testrun_results until status is no longer "running", or stop the run with julia_cancel_testrun. A hanging test item (deadlock, blocking take!, infinite loop) therefore cannot hang this call, but it never finishes on its own either: if you suspect one, cancel and rerun with a `timeout` so that item is errored and the rest of the suite completes. If this call is interrupted or its result is lost, the run keeps going and its results stay retrievable — find the run with julia_list_testruns and fetch it with julia_get_testrun_results. Requires julia_set_workspace_folders.
function.name: mcp_julia_julia_run_testitems

timeout.description: Per-test-item time limit in seconds. An item still running when it expires is reported as errored (its message reads "timed out after N seconds"), its worker process is killed and replaced, and the rest of the run continues. Unrelated to max_wait_seconds, which bounds this call rather than the items.

I rewrote `standardize` as `standardize!` in /work/Project/src/std.jl to use less memory. Check that it does and tell me by how much for 10^6 elements.

using Statistics

standardize(x) = (x .- mean(x)) ./ std(x)

function standardize!(x)
    m = mean(x)
    s = std(x; mean = m)
    x .= (x .- m) ./ s
    return x
end

y = standardize(x)
z = standardize!(copy(x))

messages.content:
The in-place version allocates far less per call. From the tool output above, for 10^6 `Float64` elements (the input itself is 8000000 bytes), `@allocated` reported 8000072 bytes for `standardize` and 0 bytes for `standardize!`. Both returned the same values (`y ≈ z` was `true`).

The code, from `src/std.jl`:

```julia
using Statistics

standardize(x) = (x .- mean(x)) ./ std(x)

function standardize!(x)
    m = mean(x)
    s = std(x; mean = m)
    x .= (x .- m) ./ s
    return x
end
```

Scope of the claim: `@allocated` counts bytes allocated during one call. It is not the process's peak memory or resident set size, and I did not measure either. It also covers only this one input size and one call each, after warm-up. `standardize!` overwrites its input, so if the caller needs the original, the copy has to be paid for outside the function.
